sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E2764. The transcript contains recognition errors and frequent speaker changes within single events; inseparable changes are marked U. Attribution follows conversational context rather than ideology. No edited teaser replays were identifiable. Findings concern claim use in this transcript, not the independent truth of scientific or historical claims.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: maybe only in a world suffused with natural and moral evil would the maximum number of people come to freely know God
candidates.explanation: Craig proposes salvation as a possible justification and requires a better feasible world (E879–897). This could shield suffering through inaccessible alternatives, but his explicit 'maybe' also permits an ordinary challenge to Law's probability inference. He supplies a rationale; whether this initial use excludes contrary evidence regardless of merits remains uncertain.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: it's simply impossible for the atheist to show that it's improbable or impossible
candidates.explanation: Craig turns possible distant consequences into an unrestricted inability to assess suffering: reasons might emerge centuries later, and a better salvation-producing world cannot be demonstrated (E1440–1495). This explicitly neutralizes adverse observations. The ripple-effect argument supplies reasons, so this is protected reasoning rather than an unsupported slogan; its universal epistemic conclusion exceeds the illustrated uncertainty.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: we're not in a position to judge with any confidence
candidates.explanation: After Law's intervening rebuttal, Craig renews the exclusion of observed goods and evils as grounds against either creator hypothesis (E1812–1822). Unknowable sufficient reasons protect the hypothesis from those observations. This summarizes the earlier consequence argument (E1440–1495), rather than replacing reasons with a catchphrase; other arguments remain part of his overall case.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: we would not be in a position to make any sort of probability judgment
candidates.explanation: Craig answers Law's observational challenge by making omniscient purposes inaccessible to any probability judgment about gratuitous goods or evils (E2637–2644). The explicit 'any sort' blocks the evidential assessment itself. He invokes his earlier Wykstra reasoning, so the episode is a protected argument, with symmetrical application to good and evil creators, rather than a slogan.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: there's simply no way for us to know that a Provident God doesn't have morally sufficient reasons
candidates.explanation: Following Law's request for an argument, Craig again invokes consequences beyond our lifetime or location (E2665–2676). The unrestricted 'no way' insulates particular suffering from adverse assessment through unseen purposes. He does supply the Maxwell ripple-effect rationale, making this a renewed protected argument rather than an unsupported affirmation; possibility alone does not establish the sweeping exclusion.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: that isn't a belief we should abandon easily but it's by no means irrefutable
contrasts.explanation: Law treats moral appearances as initial evidence while explicitly allowing revision. His moving-Earth analogy explains how contrary evidence and an account of misleading appearances could defeat that belief; E2296–2323 renews this qualification.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: in the absence of some very good argument to deny the veridicality of our sensory perceptions
contrasts.explanation: Craig compares moral experience with perception of physical objects, acknowledges a possible virtual reality, and makes justification conditional on the absence of a strong defeating argument. This supplies an analogy and expressly leaves criticism available.
